Choosing between oiled and lacquered oak

By Ruth Ellery, 14 March 2026

The finish on an oak table decides how it ages, how it is repaired and how much attention it wants from you. Oiled oak and lacquered oak both protect the timber, but they do it in opposite ways, and the right answer depends far more on the room than on the wood.

How an oil finish behaves

A hardwax oil soaks into the grain rather than sitting on top of it. The surface stays open, so the timber keeps its texture and a mark can usually be sanded back and re-oiled in place without refinishing the whole top. The trade-off is upkeep: a working kitchen table wants re-oiling once or twice a year.

How a lacquer finish behaves

Lacquer cures into a film across the surface. It resists spills and heat far better and asks for nothing beyond ordinary cleaning, but the film is the thing being protected. Once it is scratched through, the repair is a full re-coat rather than a local touch-up.

Which to choose

Choose oil for a table you expect to live with and maintain, and lacquer for one that has to survive a household without ceremony. Neither is more durable in the abstract; they simply fail differently. Our own workshop finishes are described in the Institute finish guide.
